11278.explanation: Raw okra is safe to eat during pregnancy when washed meticulously. It provides dietary folate, vitamin K, and soluble fiber with virtually no fat. CDC produce safety rules emphasize scrubbing the pods gently under running water to dislodge fuzz, dirt, and potential soil microbes. Slice crisp raw young pods thinly into fresh salads or enjoy with a pasteurized dipping sauce.

11279.explanation: Boiled okra is strongly recommended throughout pregnancy. It is packed with natural folate, calcium, dietary fiber, and vitamin C that support fetal neural development and maternal bowel regularity. Boiling or stewing okra until tender destroys any lingering agricultural pathogens and makes its mucilage gentle on the stomach. Simmer boiled okra into hearty vegetable soups, curries, or stews served with brown rice.

11280.explanation: Frozen unprepared okra is safe and nutritious for pregnancy once fully cooked. It retains high concentrations of folate, fiber, and vitamin C comparable to fresh okra pods. CDC reminds consumers that frozen produce is not ready-to-eat and must be cooked thoroughly to eliminate potential Listeria contamination. Boil, steam, or roast frozen okra until piping hot before serving.

11282.explanation: Raw onions are safe for expectant mothers when peeled and washed properly. They provide quercetin, vitamin C, and dietary fiber that support maternal immune function and regularity. CDC recommends removing dry papery outer skins and rinsing onions under running tap water to prevent transferring soil bacteria into the bulb. Add thin slices of raw red onion to salads or sandwiches, though reduce intake if you experience heartburn.

11291.explanation: Raw spring onions and scallions are safe and beneficial during pregnancy with thorough washing. They provide dietary folate, vitamin K, and vitamin C to bolster maternal health. Because scallions grow in close contact with damp soil, CDC advises trimming the roots and washing the green hollow stems individually under cold running water to eliminate trapped bacteria. Chop clean scallions to garnish cooked soups, brown rice, or frittatas.

11292.explanation: Young green onion tops are safe to consume during pregnancy if handled with good food hygiene. They provide vitamin K, vitamin A, and antioxidants that enhance the nutritional profile of meals. CDC guidelines advise rinsing the hollow green stalks thoroughly under running tap water to flush out any hidden garden dirt. Snip washed green onion tops over hot baked potatoes, scrambled pasteurized eggs, or vegetable dishes.

11296.explanation: Oven-heated breaded onion rings are safe during pregnancy, but should be strictly limited. While the onion center contributes modest potassium, the breading and oil contribute heavy saturated fats, refined carbohydrates, and excess sodium. ACOG advises limiting deep-fried or heavily breaded foods to maintain healthy maternal weight gain and avoid acid reflux. Enjoy a small side occasionally alongside a fresh green salad rather than making them a dietary staple.

11297.explanation: Fresh parsley is safe and wholesome in normal culinary amounts during pregnancy. It supplies concentrated vitamin K, vitamin C, and folate to support blood coagulation and cellular health. Wash the herb thoroughly under cold running water per CDC guidance to wash away soil microbes, and avoid concentrated medicinal parsley extracts which carry uterine-stimulating risks. Sprinkle chopped fresh parsley over pasta, soups, and roasted vegetables for bright flavor and nutrition.

11299.explanation: Boiled parsnips are strongly recommended during pregnancy. They deliver abundant soluble and insoluble dietary fiber, folate, potassium, and vitamin C to support healthy fetal growth and prevent constipation. Boiling peeled parsnip cubes until tender ensures complete destruction of soil pathogens and brings out their sweet, nutty flavor. Mash boiled parsnips with carrots or serve them as a hearty side dish alongside lean roasted meat.

11300.explanation: Raw edible-podded peas are safe and nutritious during pregnancy when washed properly. They offer crisp hydration, vitamin C, folate, and gentle dietary fiber that satisfy snack cravings. CDC advises washing the whole pods under clean running water to remove agricultural dust and surface bacteria. Snap the stem ends and enjoy clean pods with hummus or pasteurized tzatziki dip.
